It also creates a community wildfire risk reduction program and a casualty assistance program for firefighters, and extends from 10 to 150 feet the distance from power lines within which hazard trees may be removed from federal land.

supporters.text: Supporters say, in remarks by sponsor Representative Westerman, that a forest management project now takes 3 to 5 years to complete and that the bill lets land managers act on the highest-risk areas before fires start. He says a 10,000-acre categorical exclusion, modeled on one used at Lake Tahoe, would cover an area the size of the Palisades fire with 2 exclusions instead of 8.

opponents.text: Opponents say, in remarks by Representative Huffman, that the bill leaves its wildfire programs unfunded, uses emergency authorities under the National Environmental Policy Act, and makes it harder for communities to learn about projects. Representative Beyer adds that it would overturn the Cottonwood court decision requiring agencies to reconsult on endangered species when new science emerges.

card.yes_means: Federal wildfire fuel-reduction projects up to 10,000 acres should be exempt from full environmental review.
card.no_means: Federal wildfire fuel-reduction projects up to 10,000 acres should not be exempt from full environmental review.

card.title: Smithsonian American Women's History Museum Act
card.heading: Site and mission rules for women's history museum
card.changes: Designates the South Monument site on the National Mall for the museum, though the President may choose an alternative site within 180 days. It says the museum shall be dedicated to the history, achievements, and lived experiences of "biological women" and may not depict any "biological male" as a female, and it requires exhibits to reflect, to the extent practicable, a range of political viewpoints held by women.

supporters.text: Supporters say, in remarks by Representative Steil and Representative Malliotakis, that the bill puts a museum Congress authorized in 2020 on the Mall and adds guardrails against presenting history in a partisan way. Malliotakis says the dispute comes down to one sentence, and that a museum of women's history should have women in it.

opponents.text: Opponents say, in remarks by Representative Morelle and Representative Takano, that the bill replaces a bipartisan site-only version with 231 cosponsors, drops the National Museum of the American Latino, and lets the President override the site. They say the biological women language excludes transgender women, and Takano says it could lead to challenges to other women.

card.yes_means: The women's history museum should be placed on the South Monument site and focus on biological women.
card.no_means: The women's history museum should not be placed on the South Monument site or focus on biological women.

card.title: Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act
card.heading: Foreign-controlled apps like TikTok: sell or be prohibited
card.changes: Prohibits distributing, maintaining, or hosting an application operated by ByteDance or TikTok, or by another social media company controlled by a foreign adversary and designated by the President as a significant national security threat, unless it completes a qualified divestiture as determined by the President. The Department of Justice enforces it with civil penalties based on the number of users, and challenges go exclusively to the federal appeals court in Washington.

supporters.text: Supporters say, in remarks by Representative Rodgers and Representative Gallagher, that TikTok's owner ByteDance answers to the Chinese Communist Party, and that the bill lets TikTok separate from ByteDance and keep operating in the United States. Gallagher says it does not apply to American companies, cannot penalize individual users, and takes no position on the content of speech.

opponents.text: Opponents say, in remarks by Representative Massie and Representative Kamlager-Dove, that the bill raises First Amendment concerns and gives the President broad power over which apps Americans can use. Kamlager-Dove says China could still reach user data through other platforms and data brokers, and Massie says it is written broadly enough to reach companies that are not foreign-controlled.

card.yes_means: TikTok and similar foreign-controlled apps should be prohibited in the U.S. unless they are sold.
card.no_means: TikTok and similar foreign-controlled apps should still be allowed in the U.S. without being sold.

card.title: Financial Services and General Government and National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026
card.heading: Two-bill funding package for fiscal 2026
card.changes: Makes appropriations for fiscal year 2026, which ends September 30, 2026, for the Treasury, the federal judiciary, and other general government agencies, and for the State Department and related national security programs.

supporters.text: Supporters say, in remarks by Representative Cole and Representative Alford, that the package funds the government through bipartisan, bicameral bills instead of an omnibus, cutting $9.3 billion in national security and State Department spending and cutting IRS enforcement. Alford says it keeps spending below the current continuing resolution and that the White House urged support.

opponents.text: Opponents say, in a statement by Representative Moulton, that he could not vote for a State Department funding bill that ratified the decision to shut down USAID, which he says has contributed to hundreds of thousands of deaths. He also says Democrats should not vote to fund the administration as if it were operating in good faith.

card.yes_means: Congress should fund the Treasury, federal courts, State Department and related programs for fiscal year 2026.
card.no_means: Congress should not fund the Treasury, federal courts, State Department and related programs for fiscal year 2026.

card.title: Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2024
card.heading: Adding Energy Department critical materials to USGS list
card.changes: Requires the Interior Secretary, through the Geological Survey (USGS), to add every non-fuel material the Energy Secretary determines to be critical to the USGS critical minerals list within 45 days, and counts those materials as critical minerals under the Energy Act of 2020. When the House voted, the Energy Department's list included copper and the USGS list did not; USGS added copper in its November 2025 list.

supporters.text: Supporters say materials on the Energy Department's list, including copper, are not carried over to the Geological Survey's list, which they say confuses mineral producers and leaves those materials ineligible for expedited permitting. They say dozens of potential copper mines remain untapped because of federal regulation, and that without more domestic production the U.S. would rely on imports for 60 percent of its copper by 2035.

opponents.text: Opponents say the Geological Survey's list is meant for minerals whose supply is at risk of disruption, and that copper is not at risk because the U.S. is a net exporter of it. They say listed minerals become eligible for tax credits, grants, and expedited permitting, which they say would limit public and tribal comment on new copper mines.

card.yes_means: Materials the Energy Secretary deems critical should be added to the USGS critical minerals list.
card.no_means: Materials the Energy Secretary deems critical should not be added to the USGS critical minerals list.
